I love taking care of my parents. They were the best parents anybody could ask for. They would constantly thank me and were so grateful. They spend most of their money on their first kid's medical school costs. Did not save hardly any money. However, I managed it. Managing both of them was not that easy. But I am so happy to have been fortunate enough to take care of two extraordinary human beings. I miss them dearly.

snippet.textDisplay: I made a pledge to my parents that they would remain warm in their own home until they departed this mortal coil.  💯% made it happen for my dad.  When he died 13 years ago I quit my job and moved back to my hometown to take care of my mom.  She's 97 and cognitively she is 💯, but physically very frail.  It's exhausting living my life and hers (expenses, medical appointments, prescriptions, transportation, groceries, cooking, housework, yardwork, etc).  To get rid of spammers and scammers we changed her phone number, but still get scam shit in the mail every day (I successfully intercept it--usually).  Her hearing is poor, so my conversations with her are essentially me yelling.  Out in public people misunderstand the yelling; I'm surprised adult protection hasn't knocked on our door.  The past 13 years have taken a toll on me physically and mentally, and I sometimes need people to validate how hard it is.  My family isn't very good at that.  BUT, the happiness I feel about keeping my parents in their home ultimately brings me personal pride and joy and that's ultimately all I need for validation.

snippet.textDisplay: I was the granddaughter that took care of my grandmother that started during high school.  Had to give up opportunities and peer events to cater to her elderly needs. When my grandmother passed I burst into incredible heaving sobs and a sense of relief.  I could finally be free of the shackles that held me back from living my life.  I’m a 50 year old middle aged woman looking back at my caregiving years though there were times of resentment I feel that this was God plan.

snippet.textDisplay: My parents and I went in on a duplex 12 years ago. I was only 28, but at that time was thinking about their aging future. They are now in their mid 60’s so still relatively young, but can already see how they are beginning to age mentally and physically. It was the best decision we ever made, and I know not many families are able to do the same unless you can cohabitate well. They have their apartment and I have mine. I am there to help them whenever and can withdraw to my own private quarters. The cost savings as of now are phenomenal since we pay one low mortgage and utilities as opposed to each of us living in separate homes. I take mom to do her shopping and run her errands, and I can keep up with them. We are now 4 generations living here (my grandfather, parents, my husband and I, and our two children). my 91 yr old grandfather came to live with us a year ago after he could no longer care for himself so we all pitch in to care for him. This is where it’s at for those able to do this. I cannot fathom my parents getting older and caring for them from afar. It would just be too overwhelming.

snippet.textDisplay: Having gone through my father needing 24hr care, dementia, and my mother having chronic health problems,  dealing with the elderly is not fun.   Luckily, they had a large nest egg set aside but it would not last forever, and some questions arose occasionally of "what to do when the money runs out?"  and I would have no idea, I couldn't afford to pay for their life and my life.   My father's care was 6k/month.   But luckily, and I hate to say this, death did come.   Life is a cruel mistress, it gives you so much joy when you're young, even when older you can experience emotions of grandchildren perhaps, but eventually all things will stop.  But it's not just life that stops,  it's the pain, the discomfort, and worry,  and even if you don't have faith believe they are in a better place, not in pain any more, and you'll get through this just fine.

I work a demanding full-time job, and I’m taking care of my Dad part-time, every night after work. He is in a community, $10,000 per month, but the workers can’t give him the care he needs because they have other residents too. I’ve seen other communities where about half the workers ignored the residents in need. Even in the good community he is in, it is my brother and I that do all his doctor’s care, his money and things. What do people without kids, or without kids who can take care of them - what do they do? I don’t know.

If I quit my job, then how do I support myself? I still have to eat and have basic but high bills that everyone else has. Plus I get him additional nutrition and supplements, new (actually used-eBay) clothing when his weight changes, and other items. I don’t buy myself much of anything - never go on vacation, never go to a hair salon, go out to eat very occasionally with Dad, etc. already - and it’s still a struggle. I’m trying to save, but it’s hard.

snippet.textDisplay: Financial Advisor here, please please please apply for life insurance with a long term care benefit. You shouldnt need to spend all of your savings or investments on LTC. The insurance company will pay out funds monthly once a person qualifies for LTC (not being able to perform 2 of the 6 daily living activities). Also, super important to complete your estate planning immediately. Dont wait until someone is older in age to do any of this! Im also a notary and the worst is not being able to notarize a document because someone is no longer in their right mind or incapacitated. This video put the reality back in my face to continuing having real life convos with all of my clients, for themselves and their parents 🙏🏽

snippet.textDisplay: I left Long Beach as soon as I could. My mom 89 diagnosed with dementia. She will be 91 in 2 days. She does not remember me most  days. She remembers my sister and her two kids. Won’t read, draw, watch tv. Help with anything. She is still very capable physically.  Like no joke. Naps are no way. She can stay up till three in the morning , hallucinating that there’s people in her bedroom. And literally be up at 6 AM . Demanding coffee. She hides everything from scissors to Candy to breadcrumbs to give the birds.  No clue where she gets her energy from.  Financially, she hides every single thing. In the warm months, she’ll stay outside all day long just sitting there looking at planes birds squirrels grass flowers. Absolutely crazy how this disease wipes are out mentally.

snippet.textDisplay: Looks like the lucky ones are the women who don’t have to work in their 50s or so, and can take care of their parents in their own home. But  you have a supportive husband. My mother and father took care of my father‘s grandmother and mother actually my mother did it. Until they died. My dad welcomed them all into into the home when they couldn’t live alone anymore then sometimes more than one grandparent lived with us at one time. Then my mother’s own mother and father lived with us as well until they died. now my mother lives with me and my husband. We had a modest home my dad turned the garage into two rooms in order to take care of his grandmother. I was raised this way. I can’t imagine putting my mom in a home. I understand some people have to, but I think the secret to my parents and mine ability to take care of the old folks is that the husband support the families and the women stayed home. Of course,  we chose wisely and family was always welcome to stay if they were down on the their luck and as time went on all the old folks always had a place to stay and someone to cook for them and take them to doctors appointments and be part of the family until the day they died.
